reasoning:
Both submissions make the identical functional change: in `quiesce`, the guard `cp 3` becomes `cp MAXPLY`, so the capture search stops falling back to static eval after three plies and instead runs to the per-ply frame limit. That is the right fix for the reported defect. The symptom described — an `Eval` of 108 in a construction-symmetric position, 133 at level 3, and +114 in a position where the counted exchange actually loses a knight — is the classic signature of quiescence being cut off mid-exchange: the capture is credited and the recapture falls past the horizon. A depth-3 cap on the quiescence recursion is exactly the mechanism that produces it, and the reported "also observed" facts corroborate that the fault is confined to search termination rather than movegen or eval: perft passes including the incremental eval-accumulator check, the board renders identically, and a genuinely free queen is still scored correctly at 953 (one capture, no recapture, so a 3-ply window suffices). Neither diff touches movegen, eval, TT or the accumulator, so nothing that the self-test covers is put at risk.

correctness_risk — equal at 4 for both, because the emitted instruction stream is byte-for-byte the same and I will not manufacture a difference that does not exist in the code. Neither reaches 5 for the same two shared reasons. First, `MAXPLY` is not shown, so from the diff alone I cannot confirm that its value is the true frame capacity, that it is <= 255 (required for `cp`), or that there is no off-by-one against frames indexed 0..MAXPLY-1. Second, and more substantively, `cp 3` may have been serving a second purpose neither author addresses: on a 3.5MHz Z80 an unbounded capture search with no stand-pat cutoff, delta pruning or node budget can blow the time budget or the machine stack in tactical positions, and both fixes silently raise the ceiling from 3 to MAXPLY without adding any such guard or any evidence that the deeper recursion still terminates within the harness frame count at level 3+. That risk is carried equally by both.

minimality — X 4, Y 5. Both change exactly one instruction, so neither is sprawling and I am not penalising X merely for line count. The difference is proportionality of the added prose. Y adds a three-line rationale block and amends one comment that its own change made false. X appends a seven-line essay to a one-instruction fix, wedged between the `cp` and its `jp`, and ends it with a pointer to an external "design note" that the diff neither includes nor lets a reviewer locate. That extra scope is comment-only and harmless to the binary, so 4 rather than lower, but it is not warranted by the fault.

clarity — X 3, Y 5, and this is where the two genuinely diverge. X's comment does contain the more concrete evidence: it names the actual frame arithmetic (`moveBufBase+ply*512`, `undoBase+ply*16`, the 0xD4 arrays), which is the sort of detail that lets a reviewer check that MAXPLY really is the binding constraint. That is a real merit. But it is undercut three ways. (a) Placement: seven lines of prose now separate `cp MAXPLY` from `jp nc,eval`, breaking up the compare/branch pair that is the whole point of the hunk — the reader has to scroll past a paragraph to see what the comparison branches to. (b) Internal inconsistency: the comment asserts the frames "hold plies 0..MAXPLY and no more", but the code bails when searchPly >= MAXPLY, which is the bound for frames 0..MAXPLY-1. Either the prose is loose or the constant is off by one, and a reviewer cannot tell which — a justification that muddies the boundary it exists to explain is worse than a shorter one that does not. (c) X leaves the trailing `; too deep -> static eval` in place two lines below, which is now actively wrong: the exit is no longer about being too deep to search, it is about running out of frames. A future maintainer reading "too deep" is being invited to re-impose a small cap and reintroduce this exact bug. X also introduces a non-ASCII em-dash into a file whose surrounding comments use plain ASCII (`->`), a gratuitous encoding inconsistency in an assembly source. Y states the invariant and the failure mode in three lines, keeps `cp`/`jp` adjacent and legible, and specifically rewrites the stale comment to `; out of per-ply frames -> static eval`, which is the accurate description of the new exit condition and closes the trap X leaves open.

Merge Y. The two fixes are functionally equivalent, so the decision rests entirely on which one a maintainer six months from now can read correctly. Y explains the invariant without breaking up the branch, is proportionate to a one-instruction change, and is the only one of the two that repairs the comment its own edit falsified. If X were merged instead, the single change I would insist on before landing is deleting or rewriting the surviving "too deep" comment. I would also want, from either author, a note on quiescence node/time cost at level 3+ before this goes near a timed build.

Blinding note (recorded here as the output schema has no dedicated field): X's habit of appending a long justificatory comment that cites an unshown "design note" did prompt a theory about the authoring process. I set that aside and scored only what the diffs do to the source; the X/Y split above rests on comment placement, the stale-comment repair, the boundary ambiguity and proportionality, all of which are visible in the code as shown.
